title: Multi-Agent Systems: Where Coordination Helps and Hurts
content:
Giving a task to several AI agents can feel like hiring a team, but the result depends on what each worker owns and how their work comes back together. Parallelism helps when the work can be separated and checked independently. It hurts when agents edit the same artifact, repeat one another's research, or pass an unverified assumption down a chain. The useful question is not “How many agents can we launch?” It is “Which parts of this job need different expertise or can safely run at the same time?”

Start with one agent as the baseline

Run a representative task with one capable agent first. Record output quality, elapsed time, tool calls, token use, and how much human correction was needed. If the single-agent version already meets the goal, adding roles may increase cost and failure points without adding value. A multi-agent design needs an explicit hypothesis: for example, independent source gathering might shorten research time, or a reviewer with a different checklist might catch defects missed by the writer.

OpenAI's orchestration guidance describes specialist ownership and handoffs as distinct ways to coordinate work. Use a handoff when a specialist should take over a particular branch of the conversation. Use parallel tasks when independent results can be joined later. Neither pattern removes the need for a clear owner of the final answer or action.

Split by outputs, not job titles

“Researcher,” “writer,” and “reviewer” sound tidy, but the labels alone do not prevent overlap. Define the actual deliverable for each role: a source table with claim and URL, a draft that cites approved sources, or a review report naming reproducible issues. Give each worker the relevant context and a boundary on what it may change. If several agents share a repository, assign separate files or branches and a merge owner. Otherwise their concurrent edits can silently overwrite one another.

A coordination contract should include input, expected output shape, completion condition, and how to report uncertainty. It should say whether an agent may browse, execute code, edit files, or publish. It should also define the stop condition. A worker that keeps searching because “more research might help” can consume the budget while a release waits. A result that says “done” without artifacts or checks is difficult for the coordinator to trust.

Know where parallelism pays

Anthropic's account of its research system reports benefits from decomposing broad research questions across subagents, while also describing coordination and cost trade-offs. The example supports a narrower lesson: broad, separable search spaces can benefit from parallel exploration. It does not prove that every product workflow should use multiple agents. If the task requires each worker to wait for the previous one's final answer, parallel workers may sit idle.

Good candidates include comparing independent vendors, reviewing different modules, or investigating separate hypotheses. Less suitable candidates include a single short code edit, a tightly coupled database migration, or a decision whose evidence cannot be divided. For shared state, use serial ownership or isolated branches. Run a small pilot and compare against the baseline rather than relying on an architecture diagram.

Handoffs can lose meaning

Each handoff can strip context. A researcher may say a source “supports” a claim when it only mentions the topic; a writer may treat that note as proof; a publisher may then turn the claim into a headline. Preserve the exact source URL, the specific claim, the relevant excerpt or observation, and a confidence note. Ask the receiving worker to verify the claim against the source before using it. An agent's own summary is not a primary source.

A research study on multi-agent failure modes organizes failures around specification and system design, inter-agent alignment, and verification or termination. Treat that taxonomy as a prompt for local testing, not a universal prediction of your system's failure rate. Test whether workers misunderstand task boundaries, whether the coordinator notices conflicting outputs, and whether the workflow stops when evidence is insufficient.

A hypothetical editorial example

Imagine a hypothetical publishing team updating ten guides. One worker researches browser documentation, another researches security guidance, and a third creates image briefs. The coordinator owns the release manifest and article mapping. Each writer owns one guide file. A deterministic audit checks word count, links, HTML structure, source notes, and image dimensions. A reviewer reads the actual claims and cover rather than trusting the audit alone. The batch remains unpublished until all ten articles pass and the live site returns the reviewed copy.

Now imagine two writers edit the same article because the assignment was ambiguous. The later file write may erase the first. Adding another agent did not make the project faster; it created rework. The fix is an ownership table and a single integrator, not a more elaborate prompt. This is an illustrative scenario, not evidence of measured performance.

Design for disagreement and failure

Two agents can produce confident but incompatible answers. Do not average them. Ask what evidence would decide the issue, check the source or run a focused test, and preserve unresolved uncertainty. If a worker fails or hits a usage limit, the coordinator should know which outputs are complete and which are partial. A checkpoint should include artifact paths, source references, checks run, and the next safe action. Do not label a draft as published because a worker said it finished writing.

Keep sensitive actions behind a deliberate boundary. An agent that can read customer data need not also deploy code or send messages. Grant only the tools necessary for its task and review any output that crosses into production, payment, security, or external communication. Record who authorized the action, what was changed, and how to reverse it. These are operational controls, not a substitute for evaluating model behavior.

Measure the whole system

Compare the multi-agent result with the single-agent baseline on the same task set. Count total tokens across all workers, elapsed time, failure rate, duplicated work, review effort, and quality of the final artifact. A system can finish faster but cost much more in verification. It can also produce more text while making more unsupported claims. Choose a metric that reflects the user's real outcome, not the number of active agents.

Coordination checklist

  • Start with a single-agent baseline and a reason to add roles.
  • Assign distinct outputs and file ownership.
  • Set permissions, budgets, stop rules, and evidence requirements.
  • Preserve source URLs and claims across handoffs.
  • Use deterministic gates plus human review for the combined result.
  • Record partial work and failures without calling them complete.
  • Compare total time, cost, rework, and quality before scaling.
excerpt: Use multiple AI agents only when tasks can be owned and verified separately; measure coordination cost, handoff quality, and total outcomes.
seoTitle: Multi-Agent Systems: Where Coordination Helps and Hurts
seoDescription: A practical guide to multi-agent design: establish a single-agent baseline, split ownership, control handoffs, verify outputs, and measure cost.

sourceNotes.claims: OpenAI explains specialist ownership and handoffs as orchestration patterns for multi-agent workflows.
Anthropic describes parallel research decomposition along with coordination and token-cost trade-offs in its own system.
The cited study categorizes multi-agent failure modes involving specification, alignment, verification, and termination.
